body_markdown:
When you know as many “Brougham people” as I do, you never know where the next car to write up will come from. Today’s featured vehicle is a case in point.


Last February I wrote up my friend[Ron Schweitzer’s gorgeous ’68 Fleetwood Series 75 Sedan](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1968-cadillac-fleetwood-75-sedan-boss-brougham/) (so named because the limousine, with the same body, added a glass divider between the front seat and the rear compartment) when it was on display at the Geneva Concours d’Elegance in August, 2025. In the comments on that post, my friend Dean said “I have the same configuration in a Brougham, but mine was lightly optioned for 1968, including front drum brakes.” Same year, same color.


Dean Edwards


I remembered he had several ’60s and ’70s Cadillacs, including a ’68 Eldorado and ’69 Fleetwood Sixty Special, but I guess I forgot about the Emperor Blue ’68 Brougham. I immediately emailed him and asked if he could send some pics of the car and some of its history. You see, the ’68 Fleetwood Brougham is one of my favorite Cadillacs, but I’ve never seen one in person. Closest I’ve gotten is Ron’s Series 75 and the[green ’68 Sixty Special I spotted in Freeport, Illinois](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1968-cadillac-fleetwood-sixty-special-command-performance/) some time back. And he was nice enough to send me a bunch of photos and some information on the car.


Dean Edwards


As Dean related, “My ’68 was originally spotted by me in the early 90’s, and I left my information with the owner if he ever decided to sell. He called about a year later, and I went down and looked at the car, which was in very decent overall condition and being daily driven at that point. The vendor wanted a bit too much (I didn’t have a surplus of funds in those days, or much storage), so I passed and it was sold somewhere around Hamilton Ontario.


“Fast forward to 2015, and there is this Fleetwood for sale locally in Windsor. So I went to look. It needed a bit of work, and the price was over what I wanted to pay, so I walked again. A few months later, it was listed at a more realistic price, so after some haggling, it followed me home. It needed a vinyl roof, paint and bodywork. Mechanical work included new springs, muffler, etc.


On its way to the bodyshop in 2016.


Dean Edwards


“The saving grace was that I had some 1968 parts squirreled away from my original ’68 Fleetwood, such as a rear bumper, front bumper ends, etc., that could be swapped over to clean it up. This car was nice back in the ’90s, but by now, it really needed a thorough going over. Even fixed up, it isn’t going to be in the same class as the ’68 Series 75 you’ve detailed, with some faults still remaining.


Dean Edwards


In body shop—paint and vinyl roof complete.


Dean Edwards


“Because too many cars have followed me home over the years, they’re only ever going to be #3 or touching #2 cars at best, so really running restorations, rather than mint originals. It was as I was getting into replacing the rear bumper that I noted a strange trailer hitch that rang a bell.


The car, way back when.


Dean Edwards


“I dug back through my pile of pictures taken over the years, and it was then that I realized that it was the same car seen thirty-five years ago.


Dean Edwards


Dean relayed that the car was originally sold in Canada, and was a cheapskate special. His original ’68 was fully loaded, missing only seat heaters and leather interior, but this one has only air and AM/FM radio as options on top of the regular Fleetwood features.


Dean Edwards


As loaded as these things often are, Dean shared that it was odd to see one with drum front brakes, no tilt/telescoping wheel, no PDL, two-way front seats, no cruise, twilight sentinel. The car is presentable, but does have wear on the driver’s seat, and the driver’s door card has cracks in the plastic. As you can imagine, finding replacements for these things is almost impossible when you consider all the colors used and different upholstery patterns used.


Dean Edwards


I just love the car in these colors! It’s so regal looking. And 1968 was a great year for Cadillac, with the brand-new 472 V-8 adorning the engine compartment of the entire model lineup. With a Quadrajet four-barrel carburetor, it produced 375 hp at 4000 rpm.


Dean Edwards


As the nicest “owner-driven” Cadillac of the year, MSRP was rather steep at $6899. This, when you could get a new Impala coupe for $2968. As a Brougham, it had many standard features including four power ventipanes (for the final year; in 1969, flow-through ventilation would eliminate the front “wind wings,” forever), Automatic Level Control, power windows, and carpeted, folding rear footrests.


Dean Edwards


Like its sibling the Fleetwood Sixty Special, it rode on a 133″ wheelbase, 3.5 inches longer than the de Ville/Calais models. With a curb weight of 4805 pounds. Some 15,300 Broughams were built for the model year.


The ’68 with its “plainer sister.”


Dean Edwards


The 1968 showroom literature was high in its praise, as expected, for the new cars: “Now, for 1968, the Cadillac Fleetwood Series represents the supreme achievement in grand and gracious motoring. The newly designed grille of the Brougham, Sixty Special, Seventy-Five Sedan and Limousine maintains the familiar Cadillac look.


Dean Edwards


“Fleetwood interiors feature rich rosewood paneling…Selection of any Fleetwood model will be the most luxurious and rewarding decision in motoring, for the Fleetwood is the outstanding expression of Cadillac excellence.”


Dean Edwards


True in 1968, and still true today in 2026. Dean’s car is a classic example of Cadillac style, room and comfort!
